extracted.intended_audience: Parties appearing before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (petitioners, patent owners), their counsel, PTAB panels, and PTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Standard Operating Procedure describing how the Patent Trial and Appeal Board handles cases remanded from the Federal Circuit, including timelines, conferencing, and standards for permitting additional briefing, evidence, or argument on remand. Applies to inter partes trials, ex parte appeals, and reexamination appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal: issue remand decisions within six months of mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has established a goal to issue decisions on remanded cases within six months of the Board’s receipt of the Federal Circuit’s mandate. The mandate makes the judgment of the Federal Circuit final and releases jurisdiction of the remanded case to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SOP recognizes that certain scenarios may necessitate going beyond the six-month goal. The six-month target is an administrative goal to promote timeliness, not a statutory deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties must contact Board within ten business days and meet-and-confer
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties in remanded trial cases are to contact the Board within ten (10) business days after the mandate issues to arrange a teleconference with the panel. Before the teleconference, the parties shall meet and confer in a reasonable and good faith attempt to propose a procedure on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are encouraged to seek agreement on remand procedures including, but not limited to: (1) whether additional briefing is necessary; (2) subject matter limitations on briefing; (3) length of briefing; (4) whether briefs should be filed concurrently or sequentially; (5) if sequential, which party opens; (6) whether a second brief should be permitted; (7) the briefing schedule; (8) whether either party may supplement the evidentiary record; (9) limitations on type of additional evidence; (10) schedule for submitting additional evidence; and (11) any other relevant procedural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: teleconference within first month after mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleconferences with the panel should take place within the first month after the mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the administrative norm to quickly establish the remand process; parties should prepare proposed procedures before the call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel has ultimate authority to decide remand procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the panel shall consider procedures proposed by the parties, the panel ultimately will decide the procedures to be followed on remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel will decide whether to permit additional briefing, additional evidence (testimonial and documentary), or hold additional hearings following a remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel considers scope of the remand from the Federal Circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel will consider the scope of the remand, as determined from the reasoning and instructions provided by the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope of remand is derived from the Federal Circuit's reasoning/instructions and guides whether issues can be reopened, limited, or decided on the existing record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/administrative factors: economy, integrity, efficient administration, timely completion (35 U.S.C. §§316(b), 326(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel will consider 'the effect . . . on the economy, the integrity of the patent system, the efficient administration of the Office, and the ability of the Office to timely complete proceedings.' See 35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b), 326(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although no statutory time limit exists for a re-opened proceeding, delays from re-opening the record may conflict with the six‑month goal. The panel balances these statutory considerations when setting remand procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of time and expense and the 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(b) policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel will consider the time and expense involved that permitting additional briefing and new evidence will add to the proceeding. This approach is consistent with 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(b): 'This part shall be construed to secure the just, speedy, and inexpensive resolution of every proceeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels weigh benefit of reopening record against additional delay/cost; impacts whether to authorize briefs, evidence, or hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for permitting additional briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to allow additional briefing, the panel will take into account whether the parties already have had an adequate opportunity to address the issues raised by the remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A new or revised claim construction not previously considered may justify additional briefing. A change in the law usually would justify additional briefing. Additional briefing, when permitted, will normally be limited to the specific issues raised by the remand. (See Microsoft v. Proxyconn; Dell v. Acceleron.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for permitting additional evidence (reopening the evidentiary record)
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, it will not be necessary to re-open the evidentiary record to new testimonial or documentary evidence. A party seeking to re-open the evidentiary record should be prepared to demonstrate why the evidence already before the Board is inadequate and show good cause why additional evidence is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panel considers whether the parties previously had an adequate opportunity to address the issues with evidence already of record, whether additional briefing would suffice, and how much extra time would be needed to develop a new evidentiary record (e.g., to lay foundation or resolve objections). The Board’s discovery rules govern testimonial evidence and cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for permitting additional oral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, an additional oral hearing will not be authorized. Normally, the existing record and previous oral argument will be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An additional oral argument may be authorized where new evidence is permitted or where oral argument is necessary to afford due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedure: remand for erroneous claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the remand arises from an erroneous claim interpretation, panels commonly permit additional briefing directed to the Federal Circuit’s claim interpretation but typically do not authorize new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Microsoft Corp. v. Proxyconn, Inc. (Board authorized simultaneous briefing but not new evidence); Straight Path IP Grp. v. Sipnet (authorized briefing directed to impact on trial but not new evidence). If the new claim interpretation renders rejections moot, the Board may remand to the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedure: remand for failure to consider the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When remanded for failure to properly consider particular evidence, panels have authorized additional briefing related to that evidence but generally have not admitted new evidence in trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ariosa Diagnostics v. Verinata Health (permitted additional briefing about the overlooked evidence but not admission of additional evidence). Where the record lacks evidence or examiner findings, the case may be taken up by or remanded to the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedure: remand for inadequate explanation by the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: When remanded for failure to adequately explain reasoning, panels have in some cases authorized limited additional briefing (but not new evidence) and otherwise added further explanation without reopening the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cutsforth v. MotivePower (authorized limited additional briefing); Board sometimes issues a new decision adding further explanation when the record supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedure: remand for erroneous application of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: When remand is for erroneous application of legal standards, the Board has sometimes permitted additional briefing and supplemental filings (e.g., motions to amend) and/or remanded or taken case up for correction depending on whether the legal error renders prior rejections moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Veritas v. Veeam (allowed Patent Owner to refile motion to amend and supporting arguments; petitioner could file supplemental opposition). In some instances the Board remands to the examiner if the reversal renders maintained rejections moot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedure: remand for lack of due process / denial of APA rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Federal Circuit finds an APA/due process violation (e.g., Board adopted new claim interpretation 'midstream'), panels have in some cases authorized additional briefing and additional evidence to afford a fair opportunity to respond; in other cases, additional briefing alone was deemed sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: SAS Inst. v. ComplementSoft (authorized briefing and additional declaratory evidence). Dell v. Acceleron (permitted additional briefing on untimely-raised issue). The panel may also provide new grounds of rejection or remand to examiner in ex parte/reexam contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default trial procedure: remand for improper consideration of arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where remand results from misapprehension, overlooking, or improper timing consideration of arguments, panels have permitted additional briefing to address those argument-handling errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dell Inc. v. Acceleron (permitted additional briefing when Patent Owner was denied fair opportunity to respond to arguments first raised at oral argument and adopted by Board). In ex parte contexts, Board sometimes issues a new decision addressing overlooked but properly briefed arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for ex parte and reexamination appeals (who takes up remand)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ex parte appeals and reexamination appeals, reversals at the Federal Circuit are remanded to the PTO for further action; either the Board or the examiner will take up remanded cases depending on (1) whether the Federal Circuit directed a particular part of the Office to act upon remand, (2) whether the outstanding rejections can be further addressed by the Board with explanation or a new ground of rejection based on the current record, and/or (3) whether a reversal requires further prior art searching by the examiner and/or issuance of a patent or reexamination certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may ask the appellant or parties to provide further briefing on matters of law or fact raised by the Federal Circuit. Additional evidence is only permitted upon reopening of prosecution before the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default appeals procedures mapping for common remand scenarios (ex parte / reexamination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Default treatments in ex parte/reexamination appeals vary by scenario: e.g., Erroneous Claim Interpretation — No reopening unless alternative claim interpretation renders present rejections moot; Failure to Consider Evidence — No reopening unless record evidence is entirely insufficient; Inadequate Explanation — Board provides additional explanation or reverses on the present record; Erroneous Application of Law — No reopening unless correct application renders rejections moot; Lack of Due Process — Yes, typically in the form of a new ground of rejection; Improper Consideration of Arguments — No, arguments not sufficiently briefed before Board are deemed waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are default rules; particular circumstances may justify different procedures (examples and citations provided in SOP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent and case-specific examples to guide remand decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels and parties should look to prior Board decisions on remand for guidance; the SOP provides illustrative examples (case citations) of how the Board has handled different remand scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SOP cites many examples (e.g., Proxyconn, Ariosa, SAS Inst., Dell, Veritas, Cutsforth, Warsaw Orthopedic, and various reexamination control numbers) showing how identical-sounding remand reasons have been handled differently depending on record specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on stays when petition for writ of certiorari filed
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases, absent good cause, proceedings on remand generally will not be stayed once the Federal Circuit has issued its mandate, even when a party has petitioned the Supreme Court for a writ of certiorari. A party may request authorization to file a motion for a stay of proceedings on remand; the Board will consider such requests case-by-case and may require briefing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board’s primary consideration in deciding a stay is whether the Supreme Court’s judgment would impact the Board’s decision on remand. SOP provides examples where stays were granted or denied (e.g., Shaw Industries — stayed; SAS — denied). Parties are encouraged to review appellate and Supreme Court rules for timing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOP is administrative guidance only (non‑binding)
rubrics_metrics.description: This SOP creates internal norms for the administration of the Board to promote consistency. It also provides guidance to the parties and the public regarding Board decisions remanded from the Federal Circuit. This SOP does not create any legally enforceable rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the SOP as internal practice guidance: it standardizes expectations but does not alter statutory/regulatory requirements.
